answer.summary: A “one-way door” is a decision that is difficult to reverse in practice. Shreyas warns PM leaders not to assume a feature decision is a quick, reversible “two-way door” when the build commitment and later reviews make it hard to walk back.

sections.heading: What makes it a one-way door
sections.content: The distinction is whether you can realistically come back from the decision. Shreyas describes teams treating a feature choice as a two-way door—decide quickly because they can always kill it later—but says that assumption can fail in practice. Building may take five or six weeks, followed by more time to ramp up; by the time the feature is out and the team is presenting its work at a QBR, reversing course is no longer as easy as the initial framing suggested.

sections.heading: Implication for PM leaders
sections.content: Before calling a decision reversible, consider the real commitment it creates. Shreyas says teams can otherwise make choices based on engineering availability without clearly evaluating customer motivation, differentiation, or distribution. His point is not that every feature decision is irreversible, but that leaders should not use the “two-way door” label to skip that product thinking.

judgment.explanation: The answer accurately explains that a decision that looks reversible may be hard to undo in practice, and supports this with the feature-build commitment and QBR context. However, it does not explicitly cover that the decision can leave the team committed to further ongoing work and add to the PM leader’s workload—the second expected point.
